summary: Alfuzosin is a uroselective alpha-1 adrenergic blocker used to treat the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The recommended dose is a single 10 mg extended-release tablet once daily, taken with food and with the same meal each day; tablets must be swallowed whole and not chewed or crushed. Key cautions include postural hypotension and syncope (especially early in therapy or with antihypertensives, nitrates, or PDE5 inhibitors), Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome during cataract surgery, and caution in patients with congenital or acquired QT prolongation. It is contraindicated in moderate to severe hepatic impairment and with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors. It is not indicated for hypertension or for use in women or children.
indications: Treatment of the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

moa: Alfuzosin is a selective antagonist of post-synaptic alpha-1 adrenoreceptors located in the prostate, prostatic capsule, prostatic urethra, bladder base, and bladder neck. Blockade of these receptors relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate, relieving bladder outlet obstruction and improving urine flow and BPH symptoms. It shows selectivity for alpha-adrenoceptors in the lower urinary tract.

absolute: Moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B and C) - alfuzosin levels are markedly increased
Co-administration with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir)
Known hypersensitivity (e.g. urticaria or angioedema) to alfuzosin or any component
relative: Symptomatic hypotension or prior hypotensive response to other medications
Concurrent antihypertensives, nitrates, or PDE5 inhibitors (additive hypotension)
Severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) - use with caution
Mild hepatic impairment - use with caution
Congenital or acquired QT prolongation, or QT-prolonging drugs - use with caution
monitor: Blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms, especially within the first few hours and at initiation
Symptoms of angina pectoris (discontinue if they appear or worsen)
ECG/QT in patients at risk for QT prolongation

preg: Alfuzosin is not indicated for use in women. There are no adequate data on developmental risk in pregnant women. In animal studies, alfuzosin given during organogenesis was not teratogenic, embryotoxic, or fetotoxic at exposures up to about 1200 times the maximum recommended human dose of 10 mg (by AUC) in rats and up to 3 times (by body surface area) in rabbits; gestation was slightly prolonged in rats at roughly 12 times the human exposure without difficulty in parturition.
lact: Alfuzosin is not indicated for use in women. There are no data on the presence of alfuzosin in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or its effects on milk production.
renal: Systemic exposure (Cmax and AUC) is increased by approximately 50% in patients with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment. In phase 3 trials the safety profile in mild and moderate renal impairment was similar to normal renal function, but safety data in patients with creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min are limited (n=6); use with caution in severe renal impairment.
hepatic: Alfuzosin is contraindicated in moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B and C), where apparent clearance falls to about one-third to one-quarter of normal, producing roughly three- to four-fold higher plasma concentrations. Pharmacokinetics in mild hepatic impairment have not been studied; use with caution in such patients.

major: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir) - CONTRAINDICATED; raise alfuzosin levels (ketoconazole increased Cmax ~2.3-fold, AUC ~3.2-fold)
Other alpha-adrenergic antagonists - should not be combined; additive effects expected
moderate: Antihypertensive medications and nitrates - increased risk of hypotension, postural hypotension, and syncope
PDE5 inhibitors - both are vasodilators; may cause symptomatic hypotension
Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. diltiazem) - modest increase in alfuzosin exposure (~1.5-fold Cmax)
QT-prolonging drugs - use with caution; additive QT effect observed
minor: Cimetidine - increased alfuzosin Cmax and AUC by about 20%
Atenolol - mutual increases in exposure with reductions in blood pressure and heart rate
interactions.food: Take with food and with the same meal each day; absorption is about 50% lower under fasting conditions
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction documented; alcohol may add to dizziness and hypotensive effects
interactions.diagnostics: Did not affect warfarin response or the steady-state pharmacokinetics of digoxin; hydrochlorothiazide showed no pharmacokinetic interaction

serious: Hepatocellular and cholestatic liver injury (including jaundice leading to discontinuation)
Angina pectoris in patients with pre-existing coronary artery disease
Priapism (persistent painful erection; can cause permanent impotence if untreated)

monitoring: Blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms, particularly within the first few hours of dosing and at initiation
Rule out prostate carcinoma before treatment and as clinically indicated
Symptoms of angina pectoris - discontinue if they appear or worsen
ECG/QT interval in patients with QT prolongation risk or on QT-prolonging drugs
Liver-related symptoms (jaundice) given post-marketing reports of hepatic injury
counsel: Take one tablet once daily with food, immediately after the same meal each day
Swallow the tablet whole - do not chew or crush it
You may feel dizzy or faint, especially when starting; avoid driving, operating machinery, or hazardous tasks until you know how you respond
Rise slowly from sitting or lying to reduce dizziness
Tell your ophthalmologist you take or have taken alfuzosin before cataract or other eye surgery, even if you stopped it
Seek immediate care for a painful erection lasting more than a few hours (priapism)
Report new or worsening chest pain (angina) to your doctor
pk: Postural hypotension may occur within a few hours of dosing; steady state reached by the second dose
Time to maximum concentration about 8 hours under fed conditions (extended-release)
Once-daily dosing; steady-state levels ~1.2-1.6 fold higher than after a single dose
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); dispense in a tight, light-resistant container; protect from light and moisture
pearls: Uroselective alpha-1 blocker for BPH only - not indicated for hypertension, women, or children
Contraindicated with potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir) and in moderate-severe hepatic impairment
Postural hypotension/syncope can occur within hours of the first dose, especially with antihypertensives, nitrates, or PDE5 inhibitors
Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome (IFIS) can complicate cataract surgery - warn the ophthalmologist; stopping the drug beforehand does not clearly help
Use caution in congenital or acquired QT prolongation; the 40 mg (4x) dose increased QTc more than the 10 mg dose
Rule out prostate carcinoma before starting, since BPH and prostate cancer share symptoms
missed: If you miss a dose, take it with your next meal as soon as you remember that day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your usual once-daily schedule. Do not take two tablets to make up for a missed one.
overdose: If overdose leads to hypotension, support of the cardiovascular system is the priority. Keep the patient supine to help restore blood pressure and normalize heart rate; if inadequate, give intravenous fluids and, if necessary, vasopressors, and monitor and support renal function. Alfuzosin is 82% to 90% protein bound, so dialysis is unlikely to be beneficial.
